title: The Great Dimming of Betelgeuse was caused by dust the star had just made

cover.alt: A blurry reddish-orange disc, the surface of the star Betelgeuse imaged by ESO’s Very Large Telescope, above a timeline of 2019 and 2020.
cover.credit: ESO/M. Montargès et al./L. Calçada · CC BY 4.0

body: Betelgeuse, the bright orange star in Orion, became visibly darker in late 2019 and early 2020, a change you could notice with the naked eye. Images of its surface from ESO’s Very Large Telescope solved the puzzle. Some time before, the star had thrown off a large bubble of gas; then a patch of its surface cooled, and that drop in temperature was enough for the gas to condense into **solid dust**. The dusty veil hid the southern part of the star, and by April 2020 Betelgeuse was back to its normal brightness.

slides.alt: Blurry images of a reddish-orange star cross-fade above a timeline of 2019 and 2020: the lower half of the disc darkens in late 2019 and early 2020, and the star looks bright again by March 2020.
slides.caption: Four real images of Betelgeuse’s surface from the European Southern Observatory’s Very Large Telescope, January 2019 to March 2020, shown in turn as dust veils its southern part.
slides.credit: ESO/M. Montargès et al./L. Calçada · CC BY 4.0 · excerpt

slides.prompt: Some people wondered if the fading meant Betelgeuse was about to explode. When did anyone last see a star explode in our galaxy?
slides.detail: With no supernova seen in the Milky Way since then, astronomers aren’t sure how a star behaves just before it blows up. The dimming turned out not to be an early sign.

steps.label: The star throws off a big bubble of gas
A patch of its surface cools down
The gas condenses into solid dust
The dust shades part of the star

events.text: The Very Large Telescope images Betelgeuse at normal brightness
It is back to its normal brightness
A study in Nature blames a dusty veil

slides.text: We have directly witnessed the formation of so-called stardust.
slides.attribution: Miguel Montargès, Observatoire de Paris and KU Leuven, who led the study

slides.question: What could dust thrown out by stars like Betelgeuse one day become?
slides.explanation: Dust from cool, ageing stars spreads into space, where it could go on to become the building blocks of rocky planets and life.
